title: Module 2 Mastery Gate — Bitcoin from Scratch
instructions: Ten questions. The point is the explanations, not the score. Read every rationale, even on questions you got right. Retake until passing — there is no penalty.

questions.prompt: According to the white paper, what is the single hard problem that Bitcoin is solving?
options: How to create a fixed-supply digital asset.
How to prevent the same digital coin from being spent twice without relying on a trusted third party.
How to encrypt transactions so that they cannot be read by intermediaries.
How to provide anonymous payments on the internet.
questions.rationale: The fixed supply, the cryptography, and the pseudonymity are all consequences of design choices, not the core problem. The double-spend problem is the only thing Bitcoin's invention is fundamentally about. Pre-Bitcoin digital cash schemes from the 1990s solved double-spending using a trusted issuer; Satoshi's contribution was solving it without one. Read Section 1 of the paper if you doubt this — it's stated explicitly.

questions.prompt: What does a Bitcoin miner actually do, mechanically, to find a valid block?
options: Solve a complex equation that has been generated by the network.
Decrypt encrypted transactions and validate them.
Vote on which transactions are valid using a quorum protocol.
Repeatedly hash the block header with different nonce values until the resulting hash is below a target threshold.
questions.rationale: There is no equation. There is a guessing game with one rule: the SHA-256 hash of the block header (including a nonce field the miner is free to vary) must be less than a target number. The only known way to find such a hash is brute force — try inputs until one works. This is why mining is expensive and why the cost cannot be optimized away by clever math. If a shortcut were ever found, Bitcoin's security would be broken at the cryptographic level, not the protocol level.

questions.prompt: If the total hash rate on the Bitcoin network doubles overnight and stays there, what happens to block times?
options: Block times stay at ten minutes immediately, because the protocol detects the change instantly.
Block times drop to about five minutes for roughly two weeks, then return to ten minutes after the difficulty adjustment.
Block times stay at five minutes permanently, because the rule is fixed.
Block times become unpredictable because the difficulty adjustment cannot keep up.
questions.rationale: Difficulty is recalculated every 2,016 blocks based on how long the previous 2,016 blocks took. If hash rate doubles, blocks come in twice as fast for one adjustment period (about a week instead of two), and then the difficulty is raised to compensate, restoring the ten-minute target. This is what makes the system self-regulating. It is also why short bursts of hash power don't permanently distort issuance.

questions.prompt: Alice has a single 1 BTC UTXO and wants to send 0.3 BTC to Bob. What does her wallet construct?
options: A transaction that subtracts 0.3 BTC from Alice's account balance and adds it to Bob's.
A transaction with the 1 BTC UTXO as input, an output of 0.3 BTC to Bob, an output of about 0.7 BTC back to Alice as change, and a small fee to the miner.
A transaction that splits the 1 BTC UTXO into ten 0.1 BTC UTXOs, then sends three of them to Bob.
A transaction that updates the global ledger to credit Bob with 0.3 BTC from Alice.
questions.rationale: Bitcoin has no concept of an 'account balance.' The 1 BTC UTXO is consumed entirely (you cannot spend part of a UTXO any more than you can tear a $20 bill in half and spend half of it). The transaction creates two new UTXOs as outputs: one for Bob and one for Alice as change. The miner takes the difference between input and output as the fee. This is the UTXO model in action, and it is the source of nearly all of Bitcoin's quirks around fees, privacy, and coin selection.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate description of what a Bitcoin private key actually does?
options: It is a password that grants you access to your account on the Bitcoin network.
It is a credential that the Bitcoin network uses to verify your identity before processing your transactions.
It is a number that can produce digital signatures, which the network treats as authorization to spend the UTXOs locked to the corresponding address.
It is an encryption key that decrypts your bitcoin balance from the blockchain.
questions.rationale: There is no account, no identity, and no encrypted balance. There are UTXOs on the public ledger, each locked to an address. The only thing that can produce a signature the network accepts as authorization to spend a UTXO is the private key corresponding to that address. The network has no idea who you are; it only knows whether the signature is valid. This is also why a leaked seed phrase is catastrophic and irreversible — the seed is the key, and the key is the only authorization that exists.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does a Bitcoin halving directly cause?
options: The price of Bitcoin to double.
The block reward (subsidy) paid to miners to be cut in half, while the existing supply and the difficulty are unchanged at the moment of the halving.
The total supply of Bitcoin to be reduced by half.
The difficulty to be cut in half.
questions.rationale: A halving is one line of code that fires at a specific block height and cuts the subsidy by 50%. It does not change existing balances, does not reduce supply, does not adjust difficulty (difficulty has its own independent rule), and does not directly move the price (markets may react to the halving, but that is a market behavior, not a protocol effect). The halving's only direct effect is on the rate of new issuance going forward. Everything else is downstream of how miners and markets respond.

questions.prompt: Why is the long-run security budget considered an open problem for Bitcoin?
options: Because the cryptography behind Bitcoin will eventually be broken by quantum computers.
Because the network is becoming too decentralized to coordinate.
Because as the block subsidy approaches zero, total miner revenue must come from transaction fees, and the system has never operated for an extended period in a fee-dominant regime.
Because the 21 million cap will be reached and the network will have no way to add new coins.
questions.rationale: Quantum is a separate (and longer-horizon) problem. The security budget problem is more pedestrian and more pressing: miner revenue equals subsidy plus fees; the subsidy is mechanically halving toward zero; if fees do not rise to compensate, the total reward (and therefore the cost of attacking the network) falls. The optimistic case is that Bitcoin will mature into a high-value settlement layer where fees are large enough. The pessimistic case is that off-chain solutions like Lightning will keep base-layer fees low. Both are coherent. The transition has never been tested. Anyone who says the problem is solved is overselling.

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain what Lightning is trying to solve, and name one cost or limitation that the standard Lightning pitch tends to underplay.
questions.rationale: A complete answer should observe that Lightning exists because Bitcoin's base layer has very limited transaction throughput (~7 tx/s), and that Lightning provides a layer of bilateral payment channels that allow many transactions to happen between parties without each one touching the base layer. Acceptable underplayed costs include: inbound liquidity is hard to bootstrap, routing reliability degrades with payment size, the system has watchtower/liveness requirements, most actual end-users are using custodial Lightning wrappers (which surrenders the very property Bitcoin is supposed to provide), and Lightning does not by itself fix the security budget problem — it may even make it worse by diverting fees off-chain. The point of the question is to show you have absorbed the trade-offs, not just the marketing.

questions.prompt: What did the 2015–2017 'block size war' establish about how Bitcoin is actually governed?
options: That Bitcoin is governed by a formal vote among full node operators using on-chain signaling.
That a majority of miners can change any rule at any time.
That Bitcoin's developers act as a constitutional authority and their decisions are final.

That Bitcoin has no formal governance and changes require coordinated buy-in from independently-acting nodes, miners, developers, exchanges, and users — and proposals that fail to coordinate simply do not happen.
questions.rationale: There is no constitution. There is no vote. The big-blocker faction had significant mining support and prominent developers, and still failed to change the main chain — they ended up forking off to create Bitcoin Cash. The lesson is that Bitcoin's rules are protected not by any formal mechanism but by the coordination problem of changing them. This is what people call 'social consensus' or 'ossification.' Maximalists treat ossification as a strength (the protocol cannot be corrupted). Critics treat it as a weakness (the protocol cannot fix its own problems). Both positions are coherent reactions to the same observation.

questions.prompt: Bitcoin's censorship resistance is general — it does not distinguish between transactions you would consider legitimate and transactions you would consider illegitimate. Pick one case where you would, on balance, want this property to fail (i.e., you'd want a specific transaction or actor to be censorable). Then explain why you still cannot get that exception without giving up the property entirely. Three to four sentences.
questions.rationale: There is no right answer to the case you pick. The right answer to the second part is the recognition that censorship resistance is a structural property of the protocol, not a policy lever someone can apply selectively. Adding an exception requires a privileged party with the authority to apply it, which immediately reintroduces the gatekeeper Bitcoin was designed to remove. Anyone who can censor 'bad' transactions can also censor 'good' ones, and the protocol cannot tell which is which. The point of the question is to make you feel the trade-off in your own gut, rather than reciting it as a slogan. Most people do not enjoy this exercise. Doing it anyway is the point.
